g.text: Research gives you a position.Listening gives you another perspective.

A question is a starting point.Before a committee meets, delegates studya topic, examine sources and work out whata particular position means in practice.The task is to make an argument that otherscan understand, question and build upon.In conversation, a prepared idea becomessomething more demanding. Other peoplebring different priorities and experiences.Listening closely makes it possible to seewhere disagreement begins — and wherethere may be room for a shared response.Good preparation makes that exchangemore thoughtful. It also makes the limitsof an argument easier to recognise.

Field observation offers another way in.A place can prompt questions that a briefingpaper cannot anticipate: who uses a space,which stories are visible, and what remainsoutside the frame? Notes help turn a firstimpression into a question worth exploring.Keep the two ways of learning connected.Return to the discussion with a detail, anobservation or a question from the field.Then ask how it changes the way you readthe issue, rather than treating a visit asa separate item on an itinerary.The result is a habit of moving betweenevidence and experience — with enoughcuriosity to revise an initial view.
The best questions travel with you.So does the habit of looking closer.
